claim: Circadian rhythms are generated by the cyclic transcription, translation, and degradation of clock gene products, including timeless (tim).
source: Circadian rhythms are generated by the cyclic transcription, translation, and degradation of clock gene products, including timeless (tim), but how the circadian clock senses and adapts to temperature changes is not completely understood.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about circadian rhythm mechanisms.

claim: Temperature dramatically changes the splicing pattern of tim in Drosophila.
source: Here, we show that temperature dramatically changes the splicing pattern of tim in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At 18°C, TIM levels are low because of the induction of two cold-specific isoforms: tim-cold and tim-short and cold.
source: We found that at 18°C, TIM levels are low because of the induction of two cold-specific isoforms: tim-cold and tim-short and cold.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq and protein analysis.

claim: At 29°C, another isoform, tim-medium, is upregulated.
source: At 29°C, another isoform, tim-medium, is upregulated.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased tim-M levels at higher temperatures.

claim: tim-short and cold encodes a protein that rescues the behavioral defects of tim01 mutants.
source: We found that tim-short and cold encodes a protein that rescues the behavioral defects of tim01 mutants, and that flies in which tim-short and cold is abrogated have abnormal locomotor activity.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Flies in which tim-short and cold is abrogated have abnormal locomotor activity.
source: We found that tim-short and cold encodes a protein that rescues the behavioral defects of tim01 mutants, and that flies in which tim-short and cold is abrogated have abnormal locomotor activity.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from CRISPR-generated mutant flies.

claim: miRNA-mediated control limits the expression of some tim isoforms.
source: In addition, miRNA-mediated control limits the expression of some of these isoforms.
evidence: This is supported by AGO1 immunoprecipitation and luciferase reporter assays.

claim: tim alternative splicing might act as a thermometer for the circadian clock.
source: Finally, data that we obtained using minigenes suggest that tim alternative splicing might act as a thermometer for the circadian clock.
evidence: This is based on minigene experiments showing temperature-dependent splicing changes.

claim: The master regulators, CLOCK (CLK) and CYCLE (CYC), activate the circadian system by promoting the rhythmic transcription of several key clock genes.
source: In Drosophila, the master regulators, CLOCK (CLK) and CYCLE (CYC), activate the circadian system by promoting the rhythmic transcription of several key clock genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila circadian clock mechanism.

claim: The products of three genes, PERIOD (PER), TIMELESS (TIM), and CLOCKWORK ORANGE (CWO), repress CLK-CYC-mediated transcription in an oscillatory manner.
source: The products of three of these genes, PERIOD (PER), TIMELESS (TIM), and CLOCKWORK ORANGE (CWO), repress CLK-CYC-mediated transcription in an oscillatory manner (Zhou et al., 2016; Hardin and Panda, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Post-transcriptional and post-translational regulatory processes are essential for circadian timekeeping.
source: In addition to transcriptional control, post-transcriptional and post-translational regulatory processes are essential for circadian timekeeping (Lim and Allada, 2013; Harms et al., 2004; Hardin and Panda, 2013; Kojima et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The transcriptional repressors PER and TIM are post-translationally modified.
source: For example, the transcriptional repressors PER and TIM are post-translationally modified; modification status and the rates with which these modifications take place have a significant influence on the degradation of these proteins (Ozkaya and Rosato, 2012; Hardin and Panda, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Modification status and the rates of post-translational modifications have a significant influence on the degradation of PER and TIM proteins.
source: For example, the transcriptional repressors PER and TIM are post-translationally modified; modification status and the rates with which these modifications take place have a significant influence on the degradation of these proteins (Ozkaya and Rosato, 2012; Hardin and Panda, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Modification of PER may influence its transcriptional repressor activity or the timing of its activity.
source: Modification of PER may also influence its transcriptional repressor activity or the timing of its activity (Ozkaya and Rosato, 2012; Hardin and Panda, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: Circadian clocks are able to keep time accurately without timing cues.
source: Circadian clocks are extraordinarily robust systems; they are able to keep time accurately without timing cues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock properties.

claim: Circadian clocks are resilient to large variations in environmental conditions.
source: In addition, and despite their biochemical nature, they are resilient to large variations in environmental conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock properties.

claim: Circadian neurons in the brain are organized in a network that synchronizes individual neuronal oscillators.
source: Circadian neurons in the brain are organized in a network that is believed to synchronize the individual neuronal oscillators, thereby contributing to a coherent and robust behavioral output (Mezan et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2014; Stoleru et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2003; Schlichting et al., 2016; Allada and Chung, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The neuropeptide PDF is the main neuromodulator of the circadian neuronal network.
source: The neuropeptide PDF, which is the main neuromodulator of the circadian neuronal network, is expressed in a small subset of these neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the circadian system.

claim: PDF is essential for normal activity patterns in light:dark (LD) cycles.
source: PDF is essential for normal activity patterns in light:dark (LD) cycles, as well as for persistent circadian rhythms in constant darkness (DD) (Peng et al., 2003; Im et al., 2011; Taghert and Shafer, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PDF is essential for persistent circadian rhythms in constant darkness (DD).
source: PDF is essential for normal activity patterns in light:dark (LD) cycles, as well as for persistent circadian rhythms in constant darkness (DD) (Peng et al., 2003; Im et al., 2011; Taghert and Shafer, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Organisms can quickly adjust to different light and temperature regimes.
source: For example, organisms can quickly adjust to different light and temperature regimes (Roessingh et al., 2015; Wolfgang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TIM is a core circadian oscillator component.
source: TIM is a core circadian oscillator component, and mutations in tim cause flies to have short, long, or no circadian rhythms (Rothenfluh et al., 2000; Sehgal et al., 1994; Myers et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mutations in tim cause flies to have short, long, or no circadian rhythms.
source: TIM is a core circadian oscillator component, and mutations in tim cause flies to have short, long, or no circadian rhythms (Rothenfluh et al., 2000; Sehgal et al., 1994; Myers et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TIM stabilizes PER.
source: TIM stabilizes PER, which is also essential for circadian rhythmicity, and this complex represses CLK-mediated transcription in an oscillatory manner (Hall, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The TIM-PER complex represses CLK-mediated transcription in an oscillatory manner.
source: TIM stabilizes PER, which is also essential for circadian rhythmicity, and this complex represses CLK-mediated transcription in an oscillatory manner (Hall, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The stoichiometric relationship between PER, CLK, and TIM is tightly controlled and is probably the major regulator of circadian period.
source: The stoichiometric relationship between PER, CLK, and TIM is tightly controlled and is probably the major regulator of circadian period (Hardin, 2011; Yu et al., 2006; Kadener et al., 2008; Fathallah-Shaykh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Upon light stimulus, CRY binds to TIM and promotes TIM degradation through the ubiquitin ligase Jetlag.
source: For example, upon light stimulus, the protein encoded by cryptochrome, CRY, binds to TIM and promotes TIM degradation through the ubiquitin ligase Jetlag, which results in phase advances or delays of the circadian oscillator (Lin et al., 2001; Koh et al., 2006; Emery et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CRY-mediated TIM degradation results in phase advances or delays of the circadian oscillator.
source: For example, upon light stimulus, the protein encoded by cryptochrome, CRY, binds to TIM and promotes TIM degradation through the ubiquitin ligase Jetlag, which results in phase advances or delays of the circadian oscillator (Lin et al., 2001; Koh et al., 2006; Emery et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PDF signaling has been proposed to synchronize the circadian clock by regulating TIM degradation.
source: PDF signaling has also been proposed to synchronize the circadian clock by regulating TIM degradation (Seluzicki et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Temperature has diverse effects on the Drosophila circadian system.
source: Temperature has diverse effects on the Drosophila circadian system (Kidd et al., 2015; Afik et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Flies show temperature-dependent changes in the distribution of daily locomotor activity, known as seasonal adaptation.
source: Flies show temperature-dependent changes in the distribution of daily locomotor activity, known as seasonal adaptation (Majercak et al., 1999; Low et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Flies can be entrained by daily temperature cycles.
source: Flies can also be entrained by daily temperature cycles (Roessingh et al., 2015) and are phase-shifted by temperature pulses or steps (Glaser and Stanewsky, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Flies are phase-shifted by temperature pulses or steps.
source: Flies can also be entrained by daily temperature cycles (Roessingh et al., 2015) and are phase-shifted by temperature pulses or steps (Glaser and Stanewsky, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Flies keep 24 hr periods in a wide range of temperatures, a phenomenon known as temperature compensation.
source: Flies keep 24 hr periods in a wide range of temperatures, a phenomenon known as temperature compensation (Kidd et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The adaptation of Drosophila to different environmental conditions relies on the presence of at least two neuronal circuits: one that controls the morning component of locomotor activity (M) and another that controls the evening (E) burst of activity.
source: The adaptation of Drosophila to different environmental conditions relies on the presence of at least two neuronal circuits: one that controls the morning component of locomotor activity (M) and another that controls the evening (E) burst of activity (Stoleru et al., 2005; Stoleru et al., 2004; Grima et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Under hot temperatures and long photoperiods, flies shift their M activity to pre-dawn and their E activity into the early night.
source: In the laboratory, mimicking summer by subjecting the flies to hot temperatures and long photoperiods shifts their M activity to pre-dawn and their E activity into the early night (Majercak et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Under conditions that mimic autumn (shorter day lengths and cooler temperatures), the M and E activity components fall closer together and occur around the middle of the day.
source: By contrast, under conditions that mimic autumn (shorter day lengths and cooler temperatures), the M and E activity components fall closer together and occur around the middle of the day.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila behavior.

claim: Work from the Edery lab in 1999 first linked the splicing of the per 3′ untranslated region (UTR) to seasonal adaptation.
source: In 1999, work from the Edery lab first linked the splicing of the per 3′ untranslated region (UTR) to seasonal adaptation (Majercak et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The evening advance in locomotor activity at lower temperatures correlates with an advance in the phase of oscillation of tim and per mRNAs.
source: The evening advance in locomotor activity at lower temperatures correlates with an advance in the phase of oscillation of tim and per mRNAs.
evidence: This is based on previous research findings.

claim: The shift of the clock is driven by the alternative splicing of an intron located in the per 3′ UTR (dmpi8 intron).
source: The authors postulated that this shift of the clock is driven by the alternative splicing of an intron located in the per 3′ UTR (dmpi8 intron).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous research.

claim: The efficiency of splicing of the dmpi8 intron is regulated not only by temperature but also by the photoperiod.
source: Further studies revealed that the efficiency of splicing of this intron is regulated not only by temperature but also by the photoperiod (Collins et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The effect of light on per splicing does not require a functional clock.
source: The effect of light on per splicing does not require a functional clock, and phospholipase C plays a physiological, non-photic role in regulating the production of the alternatively spliced transcript (Collins et al., 2004; Majercak et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Phospholipase C plays a physiological, non-photic role in regulating the production of the alternatively spliced per transcript.
source: The effect of light on per splicing does not require a functional clock, and phospholipase C plays a physiological, non-photic role in regulating the production of the alternatively spliced transcript (Collins et al., 2004; Majercak et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The splicing factor B52 (also called SRp55) binds to per 3′ UTR and modulates the splicing of the dmpi8 intron.
source: In addition, the splicing factor B52 (also called SRp55) binds to per 3′ UTR and modulates the splicing of the dmpi8 intron (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The per gene in D. yakuba has a 3′-terminal intron that is removed over a wide range of temperatures and photoperiods.
source: The per gene in D. yakuba has a 3′-terminal intron. This intron is removed over a wide range of temperatures and photoperiods, consistent with the marginal effect of temperature on this tropical species.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A recent report suggests that the effect of the per dmpi8 intron on midday siesta might be PER-independent.
source: A recent report suggests that the effect of the per dmpi8 intron on midday siesta might be PER-independent, and that splicing of the per 3′ UTR acts in trans to regulate the expression of daywake (dyw), which encodes an anti-siesta factor (Yang and Edery, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Splicing of the per 3′ UTR acts in trans to regulate the expression of daywake (dyw), which encodes an anti-siesta factor.
source: A recent report suggests that the effect of the per dmpi8 intron on midday siesta might be PER-independent, and that splicing of the per 3′ UTR acts in trans to regulate the expression of daywake (dyw), which encodes an anti-siesta factor (Yang and Edery, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Post-transcriptional control by miRNAs and RNA-binding proteins is important for circadian timekeeping in flies and other organisms.
source: Post-transcriptional control by miRNAs and RNA-binding proteins is important for circadian timekeeping in flies and other organisms (Lerner et al., 2015; Kadener et al., 2009; Lim and Allada, 2013; Xue and Zhang, 2018; Chen and Rosbash, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Several recent reports show a role for alternative splicing in circadian timekeeping.
source: In addition, several recent reports show a role for alternative splicing in circadian timekeeping (Petrillo et al., 2011; Bartok et al., 2013; Sanchez et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Alternative splicing is prevalent in the brain.
source: This is not surprising, given the prevalence of alternative splicing in the brain and the importance of this process in regulating the amount and type of mRNAs that are generated from a given locus (Baralle and Giudice, 2017; Sanchez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Alternative mRNA processing is co-transcriptional and usually happens because of the presence of suboptimal processing signals.
source: Alternative mRNA processing is co-transcriptional and usually happens because of the presence of suboptimal processing signals (i.e., non-canonical splice sites or polyadenylation sites).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNA processing.

claim: Many factors can influence alternative splicing, including RNA structure, RNA-binding proteins, and the elongation rate of RNA polymerase II.
source: Many factors can influence alternative splicing, including RNA structure, RNA-binding proteins, and the elongation rate of RNA polymerase II (de la Mata et al., 2003; Cáceres and Kornblihtt, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hundreds of genes were identified that had oscillating expression over the day at 18°C, 25°C, or 29°C.
source: We identified hundreds of genes that had oscillating expression over the day (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by 3′ RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Most of the cycling RNAs were temperature specific.
source: Interestingly, most of the cycling RNAs were temperature specific: only a few RNAs had oscillating expression at all of the assayed temperatures (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Only a few RNAs had oscillating expression at all of the assayed temperatures.
source: Interestingly, most of the cycling RNAs were temperature specific: only a few RNAs had oscillating expression at all of the assayed temperatures (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The sets of mRNAs that oscillated at each temperature were enriched for different Gene Ontology (GO) terms.
source: The sets of mRNAs that oscillated at each temperature were enriched for different Gene Ontology (GO) terms, demonstrating that the circadian program is temperature dependent (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: The circadian program is temperature dependent.
source: The sets of mRNAs that oscillated at each temperature were enriched for different Gene Ontology (GO) terms, demonstrating that the circadian program is temperature dependent (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the GO analysis showing different enriched terms at different temperatures.

claim: A phase advance in several core circadian components was observed at 18°C relative to 25°C or 29°C.
source: Interestingly, we observed a phase advance in several core circadian components at 18°C relative to 25°C or 29°C (Figure 1C), suggesting that the circadian clock gene expression program is advanced at low temperature.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The circadian clock gene expression program is advanced at low temperature.
source: Interestingly, we observed a phase advance in several core circadian components at 18°C relative to 25°C or 29°C (Figure 1C), suggesting that the circadian clock gene expression program is advanced at low temperature.
evidence: This is inferred from the phase advance data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The phase advance mirrors the advance of the evening activity component observed at lower temperature.
source: The phase advance mirrors the advance of the evening activity component observed at this lower temperature.
evidence: This is an inference connecting molecular and behavioral observations.

claim: Smaller phase changes in the expression of circadian clock genes were observed in flies entrained at 29°C compared to those entrained at 25°C than between 25°C and 18°C.
source: Despite the clear behavioral differences, we observed smaller phase changes in the expression of circadian clock genes in flies entrained at 29°C compared to those entrained at 25°C than theobserved between 25°C and 18°C (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: tim and per mRNA profiles were advanced at 18°C compared to those at 25°C.
source: As previously described (Majercak et al., 1999), tim and per mRNA profiles were advanced at 18°C compared to those at 25°C.
evidence: This is supported by the current data and previous research.

claim: The phase advance in tim and per mRNA levels is transcriptional.
source: This phase advance is transcriptional, as shown by analysis of chromatin-bound tim and per mRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin-bound RNA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phase advance in the mRNA levels provokes a phase advance in TIM and PER protein levels.
source: This phase advance in the mRNA levels provokes a phase advance in TIM and PER protein levels (Majercak et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There were no major changes in the overall levels of most circadian components when gene expression at different temperatures was compared.
source: Nevertheless, there were no major changes in the overall levels of most circadian components when gene expression at different temperatures was compared (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hundreds of mRNA transcripts were expressed differentially as a function of temperature.
source: From the microarray analysis, we identified hundreds of mRNA transcripts that were expressed differentially as a function of temperature.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data.

claim: Both higher and lower abundance transcripts were observed at both 18°C and 29°C when comparing to expression at 25°C.
source: When comparing to expression at 25°C, we observed both higher and lower abundance transcripts at both 18°C and 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A number of GO categories were enriched among the differentially expressed genes.
source: A number of GO categories were enriched among the differentially expressed genes, and these categories spanned a wide range of biological functions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) consistent with previously reported data (Boothroyd et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: An increase in the expression of genes encoding ribosomal proteins was observed at 29°C compared to that at 25°C.
source: For example, we observed an increase in the expression of genes encoding ribosomal proteins, genes involved in protein folding, and genes involved in metabolic processes at 29°C compared to that at 25°C.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data.

claim: An increase in the expression of genes involved in protein folding was observed at 29°C compared to that at 25°C.
source: For example, we observed an increase in the expression of genes encoding ribosomal proteins, genes involved in protein folding, and genes involved in metabolic processes at 29°C compared to that at 25°C.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data.

claim: An increase in the expression of genes involved in metabolic processes was observed at 29°C compared to that at 25°C.
source: For example, we observed an increase in the expression of genes encoding ribosomal proteins, genes involved in protein folding, and genes involved in metabolic processes at 29°C compared to that at 25°C.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data.

claim: At 18°C, increased expression of proteins involved in cuticle development was observed compared to that at 25°C.
source: At 18°C, we saw increased expression of proteins involved in cuticle development compared to that at 25°C, which is consistent with previous reports showing that cuticle deposition is temperature dependent (Boothroyd et al., 2007; Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data and citations to previous research.

claim: Cuticle deposition is temperature dependent.
source: At 18°C, we saw increased expression of proteins involved in cuticle development compared to that at 25°C, which is consistent with previous reports showing that cuticle deposition is temperature dependent (Boothroyd et al., 2007; Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Temperature greatly impacted the pattern of alternative splicing of tim mRNA.
source: We found that temperature greatly impacted the pattern of alternative splicing of tim mRNA (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by whole-transcript RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: per is the only additional clock gene that showed some temperature-driven changes in alternative splicing.
source: per is the only additional clock gene that showed some temperature-driven changes in alternative splicing, and the temperature-dependent alterations were not as striking as those observed in tim.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The temperature-dependent alterations in per splicing were not as striking as those observed in tim.
source: per is the only additional clock gene that showed some temperature-driven changes in alternative splicing, and the temperature-dependent alterations were not as striking as those observed in tim.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The per splicing pattern has been shown to be changed drastically at temperatures lower than 18°C.
source: However, the per splicing pattern has been shown to be changed drastically at temperatures lower than 18°C (Montelli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Four major isoforms were identified that were generated from the tim locus.
source: We identified four major isoforms that were generated from the tim locus (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The canonical tim transcript (tim-L) did not significantly change in abundance with temperature.
source: The canonical transcript (referred to here as tim-L) did not significantly change in abundance with temperature, but the other three isoforms did.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Two tim isoforms were more abundant at 18°C than at 25°C.
source: Two were more abundant at 18°C than at 25°C.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: tim-cold was previously described as being induced by cold temperatures.
source: One of these isoforms was previously described as being induced by cold temperatures and is called tim-cold (Boothroyd et al., 2007; Wijnen et al., 2006; Montelli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: tim-cold includes an additional intron near the 3′ end of the canonical tim mRNA.
source: tim-cold includes an additional intron near the 3′ end of the canonical tim mRNA.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: tim-cold has a longer 3′ UTR than tim-L.
source: As a result, it has a longer 3′ UTR than tim-L, but a stop codon at the beginning of the intron results in a slightly smaller protein than that produced from the canonical isoform.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: tim-cold produces a slightly smaller protein than that produced from the canonical isoform.
source: As a result, it has a longer 3′ UTR than tim-L, but a stop codon at the beginning of the intron results in a slightly smaller protein than that produced from the canonical isoform.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: tim-sc mRNA is generated by the usage of an alternative cleavage and polyadenylation site located within intron 10 of tim.
source: tim-sc mRNA is generated by the usage of an alternative cleavage and polyadenylation site located within intron 10 of tim.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: tim-M potentially encodes a protein that is smaller than those encoded by tim-L and tim-cold and larger than that encoded by tim-sc.
source: The third isoform that we identified potentially encodes a protein that is smaller than those encoded by tim-L and tim-cold and larger than that encoded by tim-sc.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: tim-M was recently described and named tim-tiny.
source: This isoform was recently described and named tim-tiny (Shakhmantsir et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: tim-M is generated by the inclusion of an intron that contains a stop codon and shares all downstream exons with tim-L.
source: This isoform is generated by the inclusion of an intron that contains a stop codon and shares all downstream exons with tim-L.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: tim-M has the longest 3′ UTR of all tim isoforms.
source: Hence, it has the longest 3′ UTR of all tim isoforms.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The isoform tim-M was present at higher abundance in flies entrained to 25°C or 29°C than in those kept at 18°C.
source: The isoform tim-M was present at higher abundance in flies entrained to 25°C or 29°C than in those kept at 18°C (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: tim-L, tim-cold, and tim-M share the same 3′ end.
source: As tim-L, tim-cold, and tim-M share the same 3′ end, they are indistinguishable in the 3′ RNA-seq datasets.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The overall levels of tim-L, tim-cold, and tim-M combined do not change with temperature.
source: Therefore, on the basis of the 3′ RNA-seq data, we were only able to conclude that the overall levels of these isoforms combined do not change with temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by 3′ RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A significant increase in the levels of tim-sc mRNA was detected at 18°C compared to those at 25°C or 29°C.
source: By contrast, we detected a significant increase in the levels of tim-sc mRNA at 18°C compared to those at 25°C or 29°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by 3′ RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The temperature-dependent differences by qRT-PCR were confirmed using isoform-specific primers.
source: We confirmed the temperature-dependent differences by qRT-PCR using isoform-specific primers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The temperature-dependent changes in the splicing patterns of tim are at least as impressive as the previously described changes in the splicing of a small intron in the 3′ UTR of per.
source: These data revealed that the temperature-dependent changes in the splicing patterns of tim are at least as impressive as the previously described changes in the splicing of a small intron in the 3′ UTR of per (Majercak et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the current data and previous research.

claim: There was a dramatic change in the distribution of the four tim isoforms over the temperature range tested.
source: We found that there was a dramatic change in the distribution of the four isoforms over the temperature range tested, from a fairly even distribution at 18°C to no expression of tim-sc and tim-cold and significant elevation of tim-M at 29°C.
evidence: This is supported by whole-transcript RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At 29°C, there is no expression of tim-sc and tim-cold and significant elevation of tim-M.
source: We found that there was a dramatic change in the distribution of the four isoforms over the temperature range tested, from a fairly even distribution at 18°C to no expression of tim-sc and tim-cold and significant elevation of tim-M at 29°C.
evidence: This is supported by whole-transcript RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: tim-M constitutes about 50% of tim mRNAs at 25°C.
source: Surprisingly, we found that tim-M constitutes about 50% of tim mRNAs at 25°C, a temperature at which the level of tim expression is similar, if not higher, than that of the canonical isoform tim-L.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data quantification.

claim: The well-characterized changes in per alternative splicing are very modest in comparison to the temperature-dependent differences observed in tim alternative splicing.
source: In comparison to the temperature-dependent differences observed in tim alternative splicing, the well-characterized changes in per alternative splicing are very modest (Low et al., 2008) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the current data and previous research, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Entrainment of flies to lower temperatures (18°C) resulted in a strong increase of tim-sc and tim-cold levels compared to the levels in flies entrained at 25°C in the brain.
source: As observed when whole fly heads were analyzed, entrainment of the flies to lower temperatures (18°C) resulted in a strong increase of tim-sc and tim-cold levels compared to the levels in flies entrained at 25°C, and entrainment to higher temperatures (29°C) promoted tim-M expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data from dissected brains shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Entrainment to higher temperatures (29°C) promoted tim-M expression in the brain.
source: As observed when whole fly heads were analyzed, entrainment of the flies to lower temperatures (18°C) resulted in a strong increase of tim-sc and tim-cold levels compared to the levels in flies entrained at 25°C, and entrainment to higher temperatures (29°C) promoted tim-M expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data from dissected brains shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: D. melanogaster and D. simulans share the same tropical origin.
source: D. melanogaster and D. simulans share the same tropical origin, but these species have become cosmopolitan, whereas D. yakuba is restricted to Africa (Markow and O'Grady, 2007; Kuntz and Eisen, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D. melanogaster and D. simulans have become cosmopolitan.
source: D. melanogaster and D. simulans share the same tropical origin, but these species have become cosmopolitan, whereas D. yakuba is restricted to Africa (Markow and O'Grady, 2007; Kuntz and Eisen, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D. yakuba is restricted to Africa.
source: D. melanogaster and D. simulans share the same tropical origin, but these species have become cosmopolitan, whereas D. yakuba is restricted to Africa (Markow and O'Grady, 2007; Kuntz and Eisen, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D. virilis is a Holarctic species that is geographically temperate.
source: D. virilis, a Holarctic species, is also geographically temperate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about D. virilis.

claim: All three Drosophila species displayed some degree of behavioral adaptation to temperature.
source: Although all three species displayed some degree of behavioral adaptation to temperature, we detected differences among them when analyzing the ratio between light and dark activity at the three assayed temperatures (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: D. melanogaster had a temperature-dependent gradient in their light/dark activity ratio, with the highest ratios at 18°C.
source: As expected, D. melanogaster had a temperature-dependent gradient in their light/dark activity ratio, with the highest ratios at 18°C (Figure 3A, left).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: D. simulans showed a significant decrease in light/dark activity ratios as the temperature increased.
source: For the D. simulans strain analyzed, we also observed a significant decrease in light/dark activity ratios as the temperature increased (Figure 3A, middle-left; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, upper left panel), suggesting that D. melanogaster and D. simulans have similar behavioral adaptation to high and low temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: D. melanogaster and D. simulans have similar behavioral adaptation to high and low temperatures.
source: For the D. simulans strain analyzed, we also observed a significant decrease in light/dark activity ratios as the temperature increased (Figure 3A, middle-left; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, upper left panel), suggesting that D. melanogaster and D. simulans have similar behavioral adaptation to high and low temperatures.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data.

claim: For D. yakuba, the light/dark activity ratios at 25°C and 18°C were not different.
source: By contrast, for D. yakuba, the light/dark activity ratios at 25°C and 18°C were not different (Figure 3A, middle-right; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, middle left panel).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: D. yakuba has reduced capacity to adapt to lower temperatures when compared to the other species tested.
source: This suggests that this equatorial species has reduced capacity to adapt to lower temperatures when compared to the other species tested; this could be because this species does not experience large changes in temperature in the wild.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data.

claim: D. virilis was more active at night whereas the other species displayed reduced activity during the dark phase.
source: It should be mentioned that although the light/dark activity ratio at 29°C for D. virilis was similar to that in the other species, its activity had the opposite trend: D. virilis was more active at night whereas the other species displayed reduced activity during the dark phase (Figure 3A, right; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, lower left panel).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All Drosophila species displayed dynamic changes in tim-cold and tim-M levels in response to temperature changes.
source: All species displayed dynamic changes in tim-cold and tim-M levels in response to temperature changes, with tim-cold increasing and tim-M decreasing at lower temperatures (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: tim-cold increases and tim-M decreases at lower temperatures in all tested Drosophila species.
source: All species displayed dynamic changes in tim-cold and tim-M levels in response to temperature changes, with tim-cold increasing and tim-M decreasing at lower temperatures (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: tim-sc was detected only in D. simulans and D. melanogaster.
source: However, we detected tim-sc only in D. simulans and D. melanogaster, which had very similar temperature-dependent alternative splicing profiles (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: D. simulans and D. melanogaster had very similar temperature-dependent alternative splicing profiles.
source: However, we detected tim-sc only in D. simulans and D. melanogaster, which had very similar temperature-dependent alternative splicing profiles (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: tim-sc appears only at 18°C in D. simulans and D. melanogaster.
source: As mentioned above, this isoform appears only at 18°C, suggesting that it might be relevant for the increased light/dark activity ratio observed for D. simulans and D. melanogaster when comparing the locomotor activity patterns at 18°C and 25°C.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: tim-sc might be relevant for the increased light/dark activity ratio observed for D. simulans and D. melanogaster when comparing the locomotor activity patterns at 18°C and 25°C.
source: As mentioned above, this isoform appears only at 18°C, suggesting that it might be relevant for the increased light/dark activity ratio observed for D. simulans and D. melanogaster when comparing the locomotor activity patterns at 18°C and 25°C.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between tim-sc expression and behavioral changes.

claim: High levels of tim-cold were detected in D. virilis at all of the assessed temperatures, including 29°C.
source: Surprisingly, high levels of tim-cold were detected in D. virilis at all of the assessed temperatures, including 29°C, suggesting that the mechanism is more complex in D. virilis than in the other species analyzed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The mechanism of tim splicing is more complex in D. virilis than in the other species analyzed.
source: Surprisingly, high levels of tim-cold were detected in D. virilis at all of the assessed temperatures, including 29°C, suggesting that the mechanism is more complex in D. virilis than in the other species analyzed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the unusual tim-cold expression pattern in D. virilis.

claim: D. simulans had a similar per splicing pattern to D. melanogaster.
source: D. simulans had a similar per splicing pattern to D. melanogaster (i.e., the intron is mostly retained and its splicing is partially increased in colder temperatures).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: D. virilis displayed no differences in per splicing over the temperature range tested.
source: On the other hand, D. virilis displayed no differences in per splicing over this temperature range, whereas the changes in D. yakuba were slight (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The changes in per splicing in D. yakuba were slight.
source: On the other hand, D. virilis displayed no differences in per splicing over this temperature range, whereas the changes in D. yakuba were slight (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The levels of the canonical TIM-L protein were significantly downregulated at 18°C compared to those at 25°C or 29°C.
source: As previously described (Majercak et al., 1999), we found that the levels of the canonical TIM-L protein were significantly downregulated at 18°C compared to those at 25°C or 29°C.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and previous research.

claim: Boothroyd et al. (2007) reported that TIM-COLD is expressed.
source: Nevertheless, Boothroyd et al. (2007) reported that TIM-COLD is expressed.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: tim-M mRNA is very abundant, but a protein of the predicted size was not detected in the western blots.
source: tim-M mRNA is very abundant, but we did not detect a protein of the predicted size in the western blots, which strongly suggests that that this isoform is not translated or is translated very inefficiently.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and RNA-seq data.

claim: tim-M is not translated or is translated very inefficiently.
source: tim-M mRNA is very abundant, but we did not detect a protein of the predicted size in the western blots, which strongly suggests that that this isoform is not translated or is translated very inefficiently.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of detectable protein despite high mRNA levels.

claim: tim-M regulates in cis the amount of tim-L produced.
source: We reasoned that this isoform regulates in cis the amount of tim-L produced. This agrees with a recent publication that identified this mRNA isoform as non-functional and probably non-coding (Shakhmantsir et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by inference and a citation to recent research.

claim: A recent publication identified tim-M as non-functional and probably non-coding.
source: We reasoned that this isoform regulates in cis the amount of tim-L produced. This agrees with a recent publication that identified this mRNA isoform as non-functional and probably non-coding (Shakhmantsir et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: The lower levels of TIM-L at 18°C compared to 25°C are not due to changes in total tim mRNA.
source: Our sequencing data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and reports by others (Boothroyd et al., 2007) indicate that the lower levels of TIM-L at 18°C compared to 25°C are not due to changes in total tim mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and previous research.

claim: The lower TIM levels at 18°C are the result of post-transcriptional and/or post-translational regulation.
source: This suggests that the lower TIM levels are the result of post-transcriptional and/or post-translational regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mRNA levels don't change but protein levels do.

claim: tim mRNA levels are regulated by miR-276.
source: Recent work demonstrated that tim mRNA levels are regulated by miR-276 (Chen and Rosbash, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Temperature-dependent changes in the association of tim mRNA with AGO1 were observed.
source: Interestingly, we observed temperature-dependent changes in the association of tim mRNA with AGO1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by AGO1 immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Binding of tim to AGO1 was very strong at 18°C, but there was little or no association at 25°C or 29°C.
source: Binding of tim to AGO1 was very strong at 18°C, but there was little or no association at 25°C or 29°C.
evidence: This is supported by AGO1 immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The temperature-driven AGO1 association pattern is tim-L/M/cold-specific.
source: This pattern is tim-L/M/cold-specific: when we examined associations of mRNAs encoding other core circadian clock components with AGO1, we did not see such remarkable temperature-driven AGO1 association changes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by AGO1 immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: tim-sc did not bind to AGO1 at any temperature.
source: This was also the case for tim-sc, which did not bind to AGO1 at any temperature (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by AGO1 immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: cry, cyc, and per mRNAs did not bind to AGO1 at the tested temperatures.
source: Some of the mRNAs encoding clock components did not bind at all (e.g., cry, cyc, and per), indicating that these transcripts are not regulated post-transcriptionally by miRNA at the tested temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by AGO1 immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Clk and vri mRNAs bound to AGO1 at all temperatures.
source: Others, bound to AGO1 at all temperatures (e.g., Clk and vri).
evidence: This is supported by AGO1 immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The association of tim-L/M, tim-cold, and tim-M to AGO1 was significantly higher at 18°C than at 25°C or 29°C.
source: We discovered that the association of tim-L/M (tim-L cannot be distinguished from tim-M as they share the 3′ UTR end), tim-cold, and tim-M to AGO1 was significantly higher at 18°C than at 25°C or 29°C (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by isoform-specific qPCR from AGO1 immunoprecipitation samples shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Luciferase levels of the transgenes carrying the 3′ UTRs of tim-L and tim-sc were high compared to those of the other two transgenes.
source: We observed no significant temperature-dependent (p<0.53) or interaction (p<0.46) effects. However, the luciferase levels of the transgenes carrying the 3′ UTRs of tim-L and tim-sc were high compared to those of the other two transgenes, suggesting that they are under little (or no) post-transcriptional control.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: tim-L and tim-sc 3′ UTRs are under little (or no) post-transcriptional control.
source: We observed no significant temperature-dependent (p<0.53) or interaction (p<0.46) effects. However, the luciferase levels of the transgenes carrying the 3′ UTRs of tim-L and tim-sc were high compared to those of the other two transgenes, suggesting that they are under little (or no) post-transcriptional control.
evidence: This is inferred from the luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Much less luciferase was expressed from the reporter carrying the 3′ UTR of tim-cold than from the other reporters.
source: Interestingly, much less luciferase was expressed from the reporter carrying the 3′ UTR of tim-cold than from the other reporters, suggesting that the presence of this 3′ UTR strongly diminishes the translation of this isoform, by affecting either the stability or translation of the mRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The presence of the tim-cold 3′ UTR strongly diminishes the translation of this isoform, by affecting either the stability or translation of the mRNA.
source: Interestingly, much less luciferase was expressed from the reporter carrying the 3′ UTR of tim-cold than from the other reporters, suggesting that the presence of this 3′ UTR strongly diminishes the translation of this isoform, by affecting either the stability or translation of the mRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: tim-sc only had a handful of predicted miRNA-binding sites.
source: tim-sc only had a handful of predicted miRNA-binding sites and was not bound to AGO-1 at any temperature, strongly suggesting that this isoform is not regulated by miRNAs (Figure 4D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by TargetScan analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: tim-sc is not regulated by miRNAs.
source: tim-sc only had a handful of predicted miRNA-binding sites and was not bound to AGO-1 at any temperature, strongly suggesting that this isoform is not regulated by miRNAs (Figure 4D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of AGO1 binding and few predicted miRNA-binding sites.

claim: Expression of most miRNAs was not affected by temperature.
source: Expression of most miRNAs was not affected by temperature (Figure 4E; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: miR-969 was strongly (~3-fold) upregulated at 18°C compared to 29°C.
source: Notably miR-969, which contains what is predicted to be a strong binding site in the 3′ UTR region common to tim-L, tim-cold, and tim-M, was strongly (~3-fold) upregulated at 18°C compared to 29°C (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Half of the miRNAs predicted to bind tim-M and tim-cold were highly expressed at 18°C and half were highly expressed at 29°C.
source: However, tim-M and tim-cold contain additional 3′ UTR regions, and these regions are predicted to be targeted by other miRNAs that are strongly regulated by temperature. Half of the miRNAs predicted to bind these tim isoforms were highly expressed at 18°C and half were highly expressed at 29°C (Figure 4F; Supplementary file 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by small RNA sequencing data and TargetScan analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A miRNA-mediated mechanism downregulates the expression of TIM-COLD and TIM-M at all temperatures.
source: This strongly suggests the existence of a miRNA-mediated mechanism that downregulates the expression of TIM-COLD and TIM-M at all temperatures.
evidence: This is inferred from the miRNA expression and binding site data.

claim: The main function of the miRNA-mediated regulation of tim-cold is to impose a threshold that blocks the expression of this protein at temperatures other than 18°C.
source: That TIM-COLD is indeed present at 18°C (Boothroyd et al., 2007; Wijnen et al., 2006) suggests that the main function of the miRNA-mediated regulation of this isoform is to impose a threshold that blocks the expression of this protein at temperatures other than 18°C, when the transcription levels of this isoform are lower.
evidence: This is inferred from the miRNA regulation data and previous research.

claim: At 18°C, differences in the expression of the canonical TIM protein relative to levels at 25°C are due to the deviation of tim transcription toward the production of tim-sc and tim-cold.
source: In summary, these results strongly suggest that at 18°C, differences in the expression of the canonical TIM protein relative to levels at 25°C are due to the deviation of tim transcription toward the production of tim-sc and tim-cold, which is under strong post-transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is a summary inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: tim-L, tim-M, and tim-cold are subjected to stronger post-transcriptional control by miRNAs than are the other isoforms.
source: In addition, tim-L, tim-M, and tim-cold are subjected to stronger post-transcriptional control by miRNAs than are the other isoforms.
evidence: This is a summary inference from AGO1 immunoprecipitation and luciferase assay data.

claim: Anti-TIM antibodies efficiently detected TIM-L and TIM-COLD but not TIM-SC.
source: Interestingly, anti-TIM antibodies efficiently detected TIM-L and TIM-COLD but not TIM-SC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, right).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A degradation product overlapped with TIM-SC, demonstrating that it is very difficult (if not impossible) to detect this isoform unequivocally by western blot.
source: Moreover, we observed a degradation product that overlapped with TIM-SC, demonstrating that it is very difficult (if not impossible) to detect this isoform unequivocally by western blot.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A clear advance in the start of the evening activity component was observed in flies that overexpressed tim-sc compared to tim-gal4 controls.
source: When kept under a 12:12 LD cycle, we observed a clear advance in the start of the evening activity component in flies that overexpressed tim-sc compared to tim-gal4 controls, but no changes in the morning anticipation (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: No changes in the morning anticipation were observed in flies that overexpressed tim-sc.
source: When kept under a 12:12 LD cycle, we observed a clear advance in the start of the evening activity component in flies that overexpressed tim-sc compared to tim-gal4 controls, but no changes in the morning anticipation (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: In DD, overexpression of TIM-SC led to more than 1 hr shortening of the period compared to the control.
source: This, together with the fact that in DD overexpression of TIM-SC led to more than 1 hr shortening of the period compared to the control (Figure 5D), suggests a role for tim-sc mRNA and protein in the behavioral advance observed in wild-type flies at 18°C.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: tim-sc mRNA and protein have a role in the behavioral advance observed in wild-type flies at 18°C.
source: This, together with the fact that in DD overexpression of TIM-SC led to more than 1 hr shortening of the period compared to the control (Figure 5D), suggests a role for tim-sc mRNA and protein in the behavioral advance observed in wild-type flies at 18°C.
evidence: This is inferred from the overexpression behavioral data.

claim: Overexpression of TIM-L at 25°C resulted in a high percentage of flies with long, weak, or no rhythms in DD conditions.
source: In agreement with the results described by Yang and Sehgal (2001), overexpression of TIM-L at 25°C resulted in a high percentage of flies with long, weak, or no rhythms in DD conditions (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D and previous research.

claim: Overexpression of TIM-COLD resulted in slightly weaker and/or longer rhythms, although to a lesser degree than is observed upon TIM-L overexpression.
source: Overexpression of TIM-COLD also resulted in slightly weaker and/or longer rhythms, although to a lesser degree than is observed upon TIM-L overexpression.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TIM-L and TIM-COLD are not fully equivalent.
source: This suggests that the two proteins are not fully equivalent, even though both are functional.
evidence: This is inferred from the different behavioral effects of overexpressing TIM-L and TIM-COLD.

claim: Overexpression of TIM-M did not significantly change the locomotor activity pattern in either LD or DD.
source: Surprisingly, overexpression of TIM-M did not significantly change the locomotor activity pattern in either LD or DD, suggesting that this protein is non-functional (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TIM-M protein is non-functional.
source: Surprisingly, overexpression of TIM-M did not significantly change the locomotor activity pattern in either LD or DD, suggesting that this protein is non-functional (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of behavioral effects upon TIM-M overexpression.

claim: TIM-L partially rescued the behavioral rhythms of tim01 mutants.
source: As previously reported (Ousley et al., 1998), TIM-L partially rescued the behavioral rhythms of tim01 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue data and previous research.

claim: The rescue of tim01 mutants by TIM-L was not total, probably because of the high level of expression of the UAS-TIM transgene.
source: The rescue was not total, probably because of the high level of expression of the UAS-TIM transgene.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the partial rescue.

claim: TIM-SC rescued the rhythms of tim01 flies both in LD and in DD.
source: Interestingly, we found that TIM-SC also rescued the rhythms of tim01 flies both in LD and in DD.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In LD, expression of the tim-sc RNA resulted in the rescue of the behavioral rhythms (evening anticipation) in more than 60% of the flies.
source: In LD, expression of the tim-sc RNA resulted in the rescue of the behavioral rhythms (evening anticipation) in more than 60% of the flies (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: More than 40% of tim01 flies expressing tim-sc displayed rhythmic behavior in DD.
source: Moreover, more than 40% of flies displayed rhythmic behavior in DD.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 6B–C.

claim: Most of the rescued tim01 flies expressing tim-sc have a shorter period than the flies rescued with the canonical isoform.
source: Most of these rescued flies have a shorter period than the flies rescued with the canonical isoform (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 6B–C.

claim: Despite its smaller size, the protein produced from tim-sc is functional.
source: These results demonstrate that, despite its smaller size, the protein produced from tim-sc is functional.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of tim01 mutants by TIM-SC.

claim: TIM-L strongly stabilized PER.
source: As previously described (Nawathean and Rosbash, 2004), TIM-L strongly stabilized PER (Figure 6D, top).
evidence: This is supported by co-transfection experiments in S2 cells shown in Figure 6D and previous research.

claim: The expression of TIM-SC did not result in PER stabilization.
source: However, the expression of TIM-SC did not result in PER stabilization (Figure 6D, top).
evidence: This is supported by co-transfection experiments in S2 cells shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both TIM-L and TIM-SC bound to PER.
source: Interestingly, we found that both TIM-L and TIM-SC bound to PER (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: TIM-SC bound to PER even in presence of TIM-L.
source: Moreover, TIM-SC bound to PER even in presence of TIM-L (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: TIM-SC might function independently of PER.
source: These results suggest that TIM-SC might function independently of PER.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TIM-SC binds but does not stabilize PER.

claim: A small fraction (~19%) of the per01 flies overexpressing TIM-SC showed a peak of activity resembling the evening activity component.
source: Interestingly, we observed that a small fraction (∼19%) of the per01 flies overexpressing TIM-SC did indeed show a peak of activity resembling the evening activity component (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that TIM-SC could alter behavior in a PER-independent way, at least in some conditions.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: TIM-SC could alter behavior in a PER-independent way, at least in some conditions.
source: Interestingly, we observed that a small fraction (∼19%) of the per01 flies overexpressing TIM-SC did indeed show a peak of activity resembling the evening activity component (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that TIM-SC could alter behavior in a PER-independent way, at least in some conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial rescue of per01 flies by TIM-SC overexpression.

claim: No rescue of the behavioral rhythmicity of per01 flies by overexpression of TIM-SC was observed in DD conditions.
source: Importantly, we did not observe any type of rescue of the behavioral rhythmicity of per01 flies by overexpression of TIM-SC in DD conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: TIM-SC and TIM-L act by two different mechanisms.
source: From these results, we concluded that TIM-SC and TIM-L act by two different mechanisms and that TIM-SC is less dependent on PER function.
evidence: This is inferred from the different effects of TIM-SC and TIM-L on PER stabilization and behavior.

claim: TIM-SC is less dependent on PER function.
source: From these results, we concluded that TIM-SC and TIM-L act by two different mechanisms and that TIM-SC is less dependent on PER function.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial rescue of per01 flies by TIM-SC.

claim: 40A flies do not express tim-sc at any temperature.
source: As expected, these flies do not express tim-sc at any temperature as shown by qRT-PCR (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Isogenic control flies had an increased day/night activity ratio after transfer to 18°C in comparison to the flies maintained at 25°C.
source: Isogenic control flies had an increased day/night activity ratio after transfer to 18°C in comparison to the flies maintained at 25°C and an advance of the evening behavioral component (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C–E.

claim: Isogenic control flies had an advance of the evening behavioral component at 18°C.
source: Isogenic control flies had an increased day/night activity ratio after transfer to 18°C in comparison to the flies maintained at 25°C and an advance of the evening behavioral component (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C–E.

claim: 40A flies had cold-like activity patterns of activity even at 25°C.
source: Interestingly, 40A flies had cold-like activity patterns of activity even at 25°C.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C–E.

claim: At 18°C and 25°C, 40A mutants display lower activity than control flies only at night.
source: For example, at 18°C and 25°C, 40A mutants display lower activity than control flies only at night.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C–D.

claim: At 29°C, the 40A flies were less active in both the light and dark periods, partly because of a very distinctive midday siesta behavior.
source: At 29°C, the 40A flies were less active in both the light and dark periods, partly because of a very distinctive midday siesta behavior (Figure 7D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: 40A mutants displayed a significant delay in the time of evening activity onset that was greater at 18°C but also significant at 25°C.
source: Even more importantly, and opposite to TIM-SC overexpression, 40A mutants displayed a significant delay in the time of evening activity onset that was greater at 18°C but also significant at 25°C (Figure 7C and E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C and E.

claim: The tim-sc mutant flies had levels of tim mRNA comparable to levels in control flies.
source: The tim-sc mutant flies had levels of tim mRNA comparable to levels in control flies as assessed by determining the levels of the constitutive exons 5 and 6 (Figure 7F, left).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Elimination of tim-sc resulted in an increase in the levels of tim-cold both at 18°C and at 25°C at the maximum expression time point (ZT15).
